← [Numerical Methods](./)

Source inspiration: [@mathewsSite].

The eigenvalues of an $n\times n$ matrix $A$ are the roots of its characteristic
polynomial (see [Eigenvalues and Eigenvectors](eigenvalues-and-eigenvectors/)).
Expanding $\det(\lambda I - A)$ by cofactors gives a sum of $n!$ terms, which is
impractical beyond small $n$. The
Faddeev-Leverrier method finds every coefficient of the characteristic polynomial
from a short recursion that uses only matrix products and traces. The same
recursion also produces the inverse $A^{-1}$ and the determinant $\det A$ with
almost no extra work.

The method is named after Urbain Le Verrier, who obtained the coefficients from
the traces of the powers $A^k$ through Newton's identities, and D. K. Faddeev, who
recast the computation as the matrix recursion below. It is an exact,
finite algorithm and is well suited to hand computation and computer algebra. As a
floating-point method for eigenvalues it is a poor choice for all but small
matrices; the last section shows why.

## The Method

::: {.callout-note appearance="simple"}
## Definition — Trace and Characteristic Polynomial

The **trace** of an $n\times n$ matrix $A = (a_{ij})$ is the sum of its diagonal
entries,
$$
\operatorname{tr}(A) = a_{11} + a_{22} + \cdots + a_{nn}.
$$
On this page the **characteristic polynomial** is the monic polynomial
$$
P(\lambda) = \det(\lambda I - A)
= \lambda^n - p_1\lambda^{n-1} - p_2\lambda^{n-2} - \cdots - p_{n-1}\lambda - p_n .
\tag{1}
$$
The eigenvalues of $A$ are the roots of $P(\lambda) = 0$.
:::

Mathews writes the polynomial as $P(\lambda) = \lambda^n + c_1\lambda^{n-1} + \cdots + c_n$,
so $c_k = -p_k$. The minus signs in (1) make the recursion below free of signs.

::: {.callout-important appearance="simple"}
## Algorithm — Faddeev-Leverrier

Start with
$$
B_1 = A, \qquad p_1 = \operatorname{tr}(B_1).
\tag{2}
$$
For $k = 2, 3, \ldots, n$ compute
$$
B_k = A\,(B_{k-1} - p_{k-1} I), \qquad p_k = \frac{1}{k}\operatorname{tr}(B_k).
\tag{3}
$$
Then $p_1, \ldots, p_n$ are the coefficients in (1). If $p_n \neq 0$, the inverse
of $A$ is
$$
A^{-1} = \frac{1}{p_n}\,(B_{n-1} - p_{n-1} I).
\tag{4}
$$
:::

::: {.callout-tip appearance="simple"}
## Theorem — What the Recursion Produces

Let $A$ be any $n\times n$ matrix and let $B_k$, $p_k$ be defined by (2)–(3). Then

1. $P(\lambda) = \lambda^n - p_1\lambda^{n-1} - \cdots - p_n$ is the characteristic polynomial of $A$;
2. $B_n = p_n I$, which is the Cayley–Hamilton theorem $P(A) = 0$ in disguise;
3. $\det A = (-1)^{n+1} p_n$, so $A$ is nonsingular exactly when $p_n \neq 0$;
4. if $p_n \neq 0$, then $A^{-1}$ is given by (4).
:::

The last product $B_n$ is needed only for $p_n$, and the matrix
$B_{n-1} - p_{n-1}I$ in (4) has already been formed to compute it. So the inverse
costs one extra scaling. If the whole of $B_n$ is formed, the identity
$B_n = p_n I$ is a useful check on the arithmetic.

### Why the Recursion Works

Mathews refers to V. N. Faddeeva's *Computational Methods of Linear Algebra*
(Dover, 1959) for the proof. Here is a short version.

Write $C_k = B_k - p_k I$ for $k = 1, \ldots, n$ and $C_0 = I$, so that (3) reads
$B_k = A\,C_{k-1}$. The adjugate (classical adjoint) of $\lambda I - A$ is a matrix
polynomial of degree $n-1$ in $\lambda$, and
$$
(\lambda I - A)\,\operatorname{adj}(\lambda I - A) = P(\lambda)\, I .
$$
Write $\operatorname{adj}(\lambda I - A) = \sum_{k=0}^{n-1} \lambda^{n-1-k} D_k$
and $P(\lambda) = \lambda^n - \sum_{k=1}^{n} q_k \lambda^{n-k}$ with, for the moment,
unknown $q_k$. Matching powers of $\lambda$ gives
$$
D_0 = I, \qquad D_k = A D_{k-1} - q_k I \quad (1 \le k \le n-1), \qquad A D_{n-1} = q_n I .
\tag{5}
$$
To find $q_k$, use Jacobi's formula: the derivative of a determinant is the trace of
the adjugate times the derivative of the matrix, so
$P'(\lambda) = \operatorname{tr}\operatorname{adj}(\lambda I - A)$. Comparing the
coefficients of $\lambda^{n-1-k}$ on both sides gives
$$
\operatorname{tr}(D_k) = -(n-k)\,q_k \quad (1 \le k \le n-1).
$$
Since $\operatorname{tr}(D_k) = \operatorname{tr}(A D_{k-1}) - n q_k$, this becomes
$$
q_k = \frac{1}{k}\operatorname{tr}(A D_{k-1}),
$$
and the last relation in (5) gives the same formula for $k = n$. This is exactly
the recursion (2)–(3), so $q_k = p_k$, $D_k = C_k$ and $B_n = A\,C_{n-1} = p_n I$.
Dividing $A\,C_{n-1} = p_n I$ by $p_n$ gives (4). Finally, setting $\lambda = 0$ in (1)
gives $P(0) = \det(-A) = (-1)^n\det A = -p_n$, which is item 3 of the theorem.

The proof also shows that $C_{n-1} = \operatorname{adj}(-A) = (-1)^{n-1}\operatorname{adj}(A)$,
so the recursion delivers the adjugate even when $A$ is singular.

::: {.callout-note appearance="simple"}
## Remark — Connection with Newton's Identities

Le Verrier's original method uses the power sums $s_k = \operatorname{tr}(A^k)$,
which are the sums of the $k$-th powers of the eigenvalues, and Newton's identities
$$
k\,p_k = s_k - p_1 s_{k-1} - p_2 s_{k-2} - \cdots - p_{k-1} s_1 .
$$
For the matrix of Example 1 below, $s_1 = 6$, $s_2 = 14$ and $s_3 = 36$, and the
identities give $p_1 = 6$, $p_2 = \tfrac12(14 - 6\cdot 6) = -11$ and
$p_3 = \tfrac13(36 - 6\cdot 14 + 11\cdot 6) = 6$, the same values the matrix
recursion produces.
:::

### Sign Conventions

Many texts and programs, including Mathematica's `CharacteristicPolynomial`, use
$Q(\lambda) = \det(A - \lambda I)$ instead. Since $A - \lambda I = -(\lambda I - A)$,
$$
Q(\lambda) = (-1)^n P(\lambda).
$$
In Mathews' examples the two polynomials agree when $n$ is even (Example 2, $n=4$)
and differ only in sign, $P(\lambda) = -Q(\lambda)$, when $n$ is odd (Examples 1
and 3, $n = 3$ and $n = 5$). Both have the same roots.

## Example 1 — A $3\times 3$ Matrix

Use the Faddeev-Leverrier method to find the characteristic polynomial, the
inverse and the eigenvalues of
$$
A = \begin{pmatrix} 2 & -1 & 1 \\ -1 & 2 & 1 \\ 1 & -1 & 2 \end{pmatrix}.
$$

**Step 1**: Start with $B_1 = A$:
$$
p_1 = \operatorname{tr}(B_1) = 2 + 2 + 2 = 6 .
$$

**Step 2**: Subtract $p_1 I$ and multiply by $A$:
$$
B_2 = A\,(B_1 - 6I)
= \begin{pmatrix} 2 & -1 & 1 \\ -1 & 2 & 1 \\ 1 & -1 & 2 \end{pmatrix}
  \begin{pmatrix} -4 & -1 & 1 \\ -1 & -4 & 1 \\ 1 & -1 & -4 \end{pmatrix}
= \begin{pmatrix} -6 & 1 & -3 \\ 3 & -8 & -3 \\ -1 & 1 & -8 \end{pmatrix},
$$
$$
p_2 = \tfrac12\operatorname{tr}(B_2) = \tfrac12(-6 - 8 - 8) = \tfrac12(-22) = -11 .
$$

**Step 3**: Subtract $p_2 I = -11I$ and multiply by $A$:
$$
B_3 = A\,(B_2 + 11I)
= \begin{pmatrix} 2 & -1 & 1 \\ -1 & 2 & 1 \\ 1 & -1 & 2 \end{pmatrix}
  \begin{pmatrix} 5 & 1 & -3 \\ 3 & 3 & -3 \\ -1 & 1 & 3 \end{pmatrix}
= \begin{pmatrix} 6 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 6 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 6 \end{pmatrix},
$$
$$
p_3 = \tfrac13\operatorname{tr}(B_3) = \tfrac13(18) = 6 .
$$

**Characteristic polynomial**:
$$
P(\lambda) = \lambda^3 - 6\lambda^2 + 11\lambda - 6 .
$$

**Inverse**: from (4) with $p_3 = 6$,
$$
A^{-1} = \frac{1}{6}\,(B_2 + 11I)
= \frac16\begin{pmatrix} 5 & 1 & -3 \\ 3 & 3 & -3 \\ -1 & 1 & 3 \end{pmatrix}
= \begin{pmatrix} \tfrac56 & \tfrac16 & -\tfrac12 \\[2pt] \tfrac12 & \tfrac12 & -\tfrac12 \\[2pt] -\tfrac16 & \tfrac16 & \tfrac12 \end{pmatrix}.
$$

**Eigenvalues**: the polynomial factors as
$P(\lambda) = (\lambda - 1)(\lambda - 2)(\lambda - 3)$, so
$$
\boxed{\lambda_1 = 1, \quad \lambda_2 = 2, \quad \lambda_3 = 3.}
$$
Also $\det A = (-1)^{4} p_3 = 6$.

**Verification:**

| Check | Result |
|-------|--------|
| $B_3 = p_3 I$ | $B_3 = 6I$ $\checkmark$ |
| $\det(\lambda I - A)$ expanded directly | $\lambda^3 - 6\lambda^2 + 11\lambda - 6$ $\checkmark$ |
| $P(1),\ P(2),\ P(3)$ | $0,\ 0,\ 0$ $\checkmark$ |
| $\lambda_1 + \lambda_2 + \lambda_3 = \operatorname{tr}A$ | $6 = 6$ $\checkmark$ |
| $\lambda_1\lambda_2\lambda_3 = \det A$ | $6 = 6$ $\checkmark$ |
| $A\,A^{-1}$ | $I$ (this is $B_3/p_3$) $\checkmark$ |
| $A^{-1}$ by Gauss–Jordan elimination | same matrix $\checkmark$ |

These values agree with Mathews' worked solution. Mathews also expands
$Q(\lambda) = \det(A - \lambda I) = 6 - 11\lambda + 6\lambda^2 - \lambda^3$ by
determinants and solves $Q(\lambda) = 0$ to get $\lambda = 1, 2, 3$; this $Q$ is
$-P(\lambda)$ because $n = 3$ is odd.

## Example 2 — A $4\times 4$ Symmetric Matrix

Find the characteristic polynomial, inverse and eigenvalues of
$$
A = \begin{pmatrix} 8 & -1 & 3 & -1 \\ -1 & 6 & 2 & 0 \\ 3 & 2 & 9 & 1 \\ -1 & 0 & 1 & 7 \end{pmatrix}.
$$

**Step 1**: $B_1 = A$ and $p_1 = 8 + 6 + 9 + 7 = 30$.

**Step 2**:
$$
B_2 = A\,(B_1 - 30I)
= \begin{pmatrix} -165 & 22 & -42 & 18 \\ 22 & -139 & -33 & 3 \\ -42 & -33 & -175 & -17 \\ 18 & 3 & -17 & -159 \end{pmatrix},
\qquad p_2 = \tfrac12(-638) = -319 .
$$

**Step 3**:
$$
B_3 = A\,(B_2 + 319I)
= \begin{pmatrix} 1066 & -106 & 146 & -70 \\ -106 & 992 & 132 & -34 \\ 146 & 132 & 1087 & 67 \\ -70 & -34 & 67 & 1085 \end{pmatrix},
\qquad p_3 = \tfrac13(4230) = 1410 .
$$

**Step 4**:
$$
B_4 = A\,(B_3 - 1410I)
= \begin{pmatrix} -2138 & 0 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & -2138 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & -2138 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 0 & -2138 \end{pmatrix},
\qquad p_4 = \tfrac14(-8552) = -2138 .
$$

**Characteristic polynomial**:
$$
P(\lambda) = \lambda^4 - 30\lambda^3 + 319\lambda^2 - 1410\lambda + 2138 .
$$

**Inverse**: from (4) with $p_4 = -2138$,
$$
A^{-1} = -\frac{1}{2138}\,(B_3 - 1410I)
= -\frac{1}{2138}\begin{pmatrix} -344 & -106 & 146 & -70 \\ -106 & -418 & 132 & -34 \\ 146 & 132 & -323 & 67 \\ -70 & -34 & 67 & -325 \end{pmatrix}
= \frac{1}{2138}\begin{pmatrix} 344 & 106 & -146 & 70 \\ 106 & 418 & -132 & 34 \\ -146 & -132 & 323 & -67 \\ 70 & 34 & -67 & 325 \end{pmatrix}.
$$
Since $2138 = 2\cdot 1069$, the entries with an even numerator reduce, for example
$344/2138 = 172/1069$; Mathews prints the matrix in that reduced form.

**Eigenvalues**: this quartic does not factor over the rationals, but the shift
$\lambda = \mu + \tfrac{15}{2}$ (one quarter of $p_1$) removes both odd powers:
$$
P\!\left(\mu + \tfrac{15}{2}\right) = \mu^4 - \tfrac{37}{2}\mu^2 + \tfrac{233}{16}.
$$
This is a quadratic in $\mu^2$ with roots $\mu^2 = \tfrac{37}{4} \pm \sqrt{71}$, so
$$
\lambda = \frac{15}{2} \pm \frac12\sqrt{37 \pm 4\sqrt{71}} ,
$$
that is,
$$
\boxed{\lambda_1 \approx 3.295699, \quad \lambda_2 \approx 6.592338, \quad \lambda_3 \approx 8.407662, \quad \lambda_4 \approx 11.704301.}
$$
All four are real, as they must be because $A$ is symmetric. They are also
positive: each row of $A$ has a diagonal entry larger than the sum of the absolute
values of its other entries, so by Gershgorin's theorem every eigenvalue lies in
$[3, 15]$. Also $\det A = (-1)^5 p_4 = 2138$.

**Verification:**

| Check | Result |
|-------|--------|
| $B_4 = p_4 I$ | $B_4 = -2138\,I$ $\checkmark$ |
| $\det(\lambda I - A)$ expanded directly | $\lambda^4 - 30\lambda^3 + 319\lambda^2 - 1410\lambda + 2138$ $\checkmark$ |
| $P(\lambda_i)$ for the four closed-form roots | $0$ exactly $\checkmark$ |
| $\lambda_1 + \cdots + \lambda_4 = \operatorname{tr}A$ | $30$ $\checkmark$ |
| $\lambda_1\lambda_2\lambda_3\lambda_4 = \det A$ | $2138$ $\checkmark$ |
| Eigenvalues by a standard eigenvalue routine (LAPACK) | $3.295699,\ 6.592338,\ 8.407662,\ 11.704301$ $\checkmark$ |
| $A^{-1}$ by Gauss–Jordan elimination | same matrix $\checkmark$ |

The matrices $B_2$, $B_3$, $B_4$, the coefficients and the inverse agree with
Mathews' worked solution. Because $n = 4$ is even, $\det(A - \lambda I)$ is the same
polynomial as $P(\lambda)$.

## Example 3 — A $5\times 5$ Tridiagonal Matrix

Find the characteristic polynomial, inverse and eigenvalues of
$$
A = \begin{pmatrix} 2 & 1 & 0 & 0 & 0 \\ 1 & 2 & 1 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 & 2 & 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 1 & 2 & 1 \\ 0 & 0 & 0 & 1 & 2 \end{pmatrix}.
$$

The output images of Mathews' solution to this example are missing from the
archive, so every number below is our own exact computation.

**Step 1**: $B_1 = A$ and $p_1 = 10$.

**Step 2**:
$$
B_2 = A\,(B_1 - 10I)
= \begin{pmatrix} -15 & -6 & 1 & 0 & 0 \\ -6 & -14 & -6 & 1 & 0 \\ 1 & -6 & -14 & -6 & 1 \\ 0 & 1 & -6 & -14 & -6 \\ 0 & 0 & 1 & -6 & -15 \end{pmatrix},
\qquad p_2 = \tfrac12(-72) = -36 .
$$

**Step 3**:
$$
B_3 = A\,(B_2 + 36I)
= \begin{pmatrix} 36 & 10 & -4 & 1 & 0 \\ 10 & 32 & 11 & -4 & 1 \\ -4 & 11 & 32 & 11 & -4 \\ 1 & -4 & 11 & 32 & 10 \\ 0 & 1 & -4 & 10 & 36 \end{pmatrix},
\qquad p_3 = \tfrac13(168) = 56 .
$$

**Step 4**:
$$
B_4 = A\,(B_3 - 56I)
= \begin{pmatrix} -30 & -4 & 3 & -2 & 1 \\ -4 & -27 & -6 & 4 & -2 \\ 3 & -6 & -26 & -6 & 3 \\ -2 & 4 & -6 & -27 & -4 \\ 1 & -2 & 3 & -4 & -30 \end{pmatrix},
\qquad p_4 = \tfrac14(-140) = -35 .
$$

**Step 5**:
$$
B_5 = A\,(B_4 + 35I) = 6I,
\qquad p_5 = \tfrac15(30) = 6 .
$$

**Characteristic polynomial**:
$$
P(\lambda) = \lambda^5 - 10\lambda^4 + 36\lambda^3 - 56\lambda^2 + 35\lambda - 6 .
$$

**Inverse**: from (4) with $p_5 = 6$,
$$
A^{-1} = \frac16\,(B_4 + 35I)
= \frac16\begin{pmatrix} 5 & -4 & 3 & -2 & 1 \\ -4 & 8 & -6 & 4 & -2 \\ 3 & -6 & 9 & -6 & 3 \\ -2 & 4 & -6 & 8 & -4 \\ 1 & -2 & 3 & -4 & 5 \end{pmatrix}.
$$
This matches the known formula for this tridiagonal matrix,
$(A^{-1})_{ij} = (-1)^{i+j}\,\min(i,j)\,\bigl(6 - \max(i,j)\bigr)/6$.

**Eigenvalues**: the polynomial factors as
$$
P(\lambda) = (\lambda - 1)(\lambda - 2)(\lambda - 3)(\lambda^2 - 4\lambda + 1),
$$
so
$$
\boxed{\lambda = 2 - \sqrt3 \approx 0.267949, \quad 1, \quad 2, \quad 3, \quad 2 + \sqrt3 \approx 3.732051.}
$$
These are the values $2 + 2\cos\!\bigl(k\pi/6\bigr)$, $k = 1, \ldots, 5$, given by the
standard formula for the eigenvalues of this tridiagonal matrix.

**Verification:**

| Check | Result |
|-------|--------|
| $B_5 = p_5 I$ | $B_5 = 6I$ $\checkmark$ |
| $\det(\lambda I - A)$ expanded directly | $\lambda^5 - 10\lambda^4 + 36\lambda^3 - 56\lambda^2 + 35\lambda - 6$ $\checkmark$ |
| $P(\lambda_i)$ for the five roots | $0$ exactly $\checkmark$ |
| $\sum\lambda_i = \operatorname{tr}A$ | $10$ $\checkmark$ |
| $\prod\lambda_i = \det A = (-1)^6 p_5$ | $6$ $\checkmark$ |
| $A^{-1}$ by Gauss–Jordan elimination | same matrix $\checkmark$ |

Since $n = 5$ is odd, $\det(A - \lambda I) = -P(\lambda)$, the sign difference
Mathews points out.

## Practical Notes

### Integer matrices

In all three examples $A$ has integer entries, and every $B_k$ and every $p_k$ is an
integer: the divisions by $k$ in (3) come out exact. This holds for every integer
matrix, because the coefficients of the characteristic polynomial of an integer
matrix are integers, and then each $B_k = A\,C_{k-1}$ is a product of integer
matrices. The method needs no fractions until the final division in (4).

### Singular matrices

The recursion never divides by anything but $k$, so it runs to completion for every
square matrix, singular or not. Only (4) needs $p_n \neq 0$. For example, $A - I$
from Example 1 is singular (it has eigenvalue $0$). The recursion gives
$p_1 = 3$, $p_2 = -2$, $p_3 = 0$, so
$P(\lambda) = \lambda^3 - 3\lambda^2 + 2\lambda = \lambda(\lambda - 1)(\lambda - 2)$,
the eigenvalues of Example 1 shifted down by one. Here $B_3$ is the zero matrix, and
$C_2 = B_2 + 2I$ equals $\operatorname{adj}(A - I)$, as the proof above predicts
for $n = 3$.

::: {.callout-warning appearance="simple"}
## Caution — Division by $k$

The divisions by $k = 2, \ldots, n$ are harmless over the real or complex numbers.
In general, the method fails in arithmetic modulo a prime $q \le n$ (where $k = q$
has no inverse); this is a general remark, not something the examples here exercise.
:::

### Cost

As a general operation count: the method forms $n - 1$ products of $n\times n$
matrices. With ordinary matrix multiplication each costs $n^3$ multiplications, so
the method costs about $n^4$ multiplications; only the diagonal of the last
product $B_n$ is needed, which saves a little. The standard route to eigenvalues,
[Householder](householder-transformations.qmd) or
[Hessenberg](hessenberg-factorization.qmd) reduction followed by the
[QR method](qr-method/), costs on the order of $n^3$ operations.

### Floating-point accuracy

The method is exact in exact arithmetic, and for the integer matrices above even
double-precision arithmetic reproduces it exactly, since all the integers involved
are small. With general real entries two separate problems appear:

1. the coefficients $p_k$ computed in floating point lose accuracy as $n$ grows, and
2. the roots of a polynomial can be extremely sensitive to its coefficients, so even
   correctly rounded coefficients may give poor eigenvalues.

To see both, we took symmetric matrices $A = Q\,\operatorname{diag}(1, 2, \ldots, n)\,Q^{\mathsf T}$
with a random orthogonal $Q$, so the eigenvalues are $1, 2, \ldots, n$. We ran the
recursion in double precision, compared the coefficients with the same recursion
run at 120 significant digits, and compared the roots of the double-precision
polynomial with the eigenvalues from a standard symmetric eigenvalue routine:

| $n$ | largest relative error in $p_k$ | largest eigenvalue error from the roots of $P$ |
|----:|--------------------------------:|-----------------------------------------------:|
| 5   | $4.6\times 10^{-16}$ | $1.9\times 10^{-13}$ |
| 10  | $2.6\times 10^{-14}$ | $3.2\times 10^{-9}$ |
| 15  | $5.0\times 10^{-11}$ | $1.0\times 10^{-5}$ |
| 20  | $6.1\times 10^{-9}$  | $1.5\times 10^{-1}$ |
| 25  | $2.5\times 10^{-6}$  | $1.4$ (complex roots appear) |
| 30  | $8.7\times 10^{-4}$  | $3.2$ (complex roots appear) |

At $n = 20$ the polynomial is, up to rounding, Wilkinson's polynomial
$(\lambda-1)(\lambda-2)\cdots(\lambda-20)$, and its coefficients range from
$p_1 \approx 210$ to $|p_{18}| \approx 1.4\times 10^{19}$. Rounding the 120-digit
coefficients to double precision and finding the roots still gives eigenvalue
errors of $0.14$, while finding the roots of the 120-digit coefficients in high
precision gives the eigenvalues to about $2\times 10^{-14}$. So at $n = 20$ the loss comes mainly from
problem 2, the sensitivity of the roots, rather than from the recursion itself.

This is why practical eigenvalue software never forms the characteristic polynomial.
For a few eigenvalues use the [power method](power-method/); for all of them, reduce
$A$ to [Hessenberg](hessenberg-factorization.qmd) (or tridiagonal) form with
[Householder transformations](householder-transformations.qmd) and apply the
[QR method](qr-method/). The Faddeev-Leverrier method remains useful for exact or
symbolic computation, for small matrices, and as a neat proof that the coefficients
of $P$, the adjugate and the inverse all come from the same short recursion.
